message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is a concise overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (as of 2026). For specific legal advice, consult a licensed attorney. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Landlord must return the deposit (or a written itemized statement of deductions) within **30 days** after the tenant vacates, unless the lease specifies a longer period. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs you pay.
• If the landlord fails to return the deposit on time, you may sue for the full amount plus damages. | | **Habitability** | • Landlords must maintain the premises in a **safe and sanitary condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• The landlord must repair any major defects that affect health or safety. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• If the landlord fails to repair, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord may raise rent **once per year** and must give **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent can only be increased at the start of a new term. | • If you receive a notice that violates the 30‑day rule, you can refuse to pay the increased amount until proper notice is given. | | **Entry Notice** | • Landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** before entering, except in emergencies. | • If the landlord enters without notice, you can withhold rent or sue for damages. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights if you suspect discrimination. | | **Lease Termination** | • Tenants may terminate a lease early by giving **30 days’ written notice** (for month‑to‑month) or following the lease’s termination clause.
• Landlords must provide a **written notice of termination** that includes the reason and the date the lease ends. | • If the landlord gives a notice that is too short or lacks a valid reason, you may stay until the proper notice period expires. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect within a reasonable time after notice, the tenant may repair it and deduct the cost from rent (up to the amount of the rent). | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the repair and the amount deducted. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Tenants have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • If the landlord repeatedly interferes (e.g., frequent unannounced visits), you can sue for damages. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Property Code** eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violation), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order. | • If the landlord skips the required notice or files a lawsuit without proper grounds, the eviction may be dismissed. | | **Right to Retaliation Protection** | • Landlords cannot retaliate against tenants who exercise their rights (e.g., file a complaint, request repairs). | • If you face retaliation (e.g., unjustified rent increase, eviction notice), you can sue for damages. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Keep Records** – Maintain copies of the lease, all correspondence, receipts, and photos of any maintenance issues. 2. **Written Notices** – Whenever you send a notice to your landlord (e.g., repair request, termination notice), send it via certified mail or another method that provides proof of delivery. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Understand the required notice periods for rent increases, entry, and termination. 4. **Seek Legal Help** – If you encounter a dispute, consider contacting a local tenant‑rights organization or a lawyer who specializes in landlord‑tenant law. --- #### Quick Reference: When to Contact an Attorney - **Landlord refuses to return the security deposit** after 30 days. - **Landlord fails to make necessary repairs** after you’ve notified them. - **You receive a notice of termination or rent increase** that violates the required notice period. - **You suspect discrimination** or retaliation. - **You’re facing eviction** and want to challenge the legality of the process. If you need a specific legal document (e.g., a lease agreement or a notice of termination), let me know the details and I can generate a template for you.
